content: The term Training Effect refers to the physiological adaptations that occur in the body as a result of engaging in physical exercise. This concept was first identified by Dr. Kenneth H. Cooper in the late 1960s while working with the United States Air Force. Dr. Cooper introduced the term Training Effect to describe these changes. Additionally, there is an increase in the total blood volume and the number of red blood cells, which enhances the blood's capacity to transport oxygen efficiently. Dr. Cooper demonstrated that these benefits could be achieved through various forms of aerobic exercise, performed according to different schedules. To quantify exercise and its effects, he developed a system of awarding points based on the amount and intensity of exercise performed. This system is detailed in his seminal 1968 book, Aerobics (ISBN 0-553-20992-2), which has been reprinted and expanded multiple times. Dr. Cooper recommended accumulating 30 points per week to maintain the Training Effect. He also introduced the 12-minute test, commonly known as the Cooper Test, to assess an individual's fitness level and guide them in starting an appropriate exercise regimen. Importantly, Dr. Cooper emphasized the necessity of undergoing a physical examination before beginning any exercise program. He also noted the phenomenon of exercise-induced hypertension, which can be evaluated through specific medical tests. Since Dr. Cooper's pioneering work, the physiological effects of exercise have been extensively studied. Current research suggests that the impact of exercise on the general metabolic rate after a workout (post-exercise) is relatively modest and tends to last only a few hours. However, various components of physical fitness—including general endurance (as partially reflected by VO2 max), muscular strength, local muscular endurance, and flexibility—are highly trainable across all age groups in many individuals. Dr. Cooper's Points System continues to serve as a useful framework for guiding exercise programs aimed at improving overall fitness.
